l: The Fort Worth Police Department recognizes that the overall wellness and resiliency of an employee has an effect on both their work and home life. This General Order is intended to address those aspects of the employee’s wellness as it relates to their work within the Police Department and to establish various resources that are available to employees to promote their wellness and resiliency. In addition, the Fort Worth Police Department employs an Early Intervention system that is designed to facilitate an intervention process that objectively and analytically identifies employees who may be in need and provides the employee with mentoring, training, or counseling.

A. The Wellness Unit creates a culture that promotes and embraces employee wellness by providing all Fort Worth Police Department employees with training, support, and resources that promote a holistic approach to wellness benefiting both the employee and their families. This will be accomplished by providing education, access to resources, spousal/family support, and post-incident follow-ups through the check-point program.
B. The Wellness Unit is overseen by a Sergeant who supervises the Wellness Unit Corporal and officer(s), Physical Fitness Coordinator, and Peer Support Coordinator.
C. Wellness Unit personnel are on 24/7 emergency callback status and shall respond to all:
3. Any request from a field supervisor with the approval of the Wellness Unit Sergeant.

Check-point personnel are volunteer members selected from various divisions throughout the department that receive specialized training from the Wellness Unit. Check-Point personnel will contact employees who have experienced critical incidents, traumatic events, or hardships. Personnel will provide support, and when appropriate, direct employees to the Wellness Unit for referral for professional services. Methods of initiating a Check-Point contact may include:
1. Police Communications Division notification of minor and major level incidents,
2. Requests from a peer or supervisor to check on a particular employee or group of employees, or
3. Notifications of injuries made by the Medical Records Unit.

Peer Support personnel are beneficial to coworkers because they come from their homogenous group; therefore, giving them an “ethos” (credibility) that no academic training program can create. Peer Support members are not counselors or therapists, but are specially-trained colleagues who volunteer their time to provide intervention and assistance to police department employees involved in traumatic incidents and in times of personal and/or professional crisis. Since performing their duties as a Peer Support member is voluntary, Peer Support members shall not be additionally compensated by the Department for duties while serving as a Peer Support member, except as noted in General Order 421.02 B.
1. The Peer Support Team is supervised by the Peer Support Coordinator who is appointed by the Chief of Police based on qualifications and training to further the mission of the Peer Support Team.

a. When employees are directed to seek assistance from the Peer Support Coordinator or the Employee Assistance Program (EAP), only the supervisor or command staff with the need to know may be informed of the employee’s compliance with the directive. No other information or details shall be provided without the employee’s knowledge and permission.

b. Conversations with Peer Support members are not protected by legal privilege however, communication with Peer Support members and employees are confidential through Police Department mandated policy, and in accordance with Texas Health and Safety Code, Chapter 784. Therefore, these conversations shall not be subject to any administrative investigation. The exceptions to confidentiality occur in cases where state or federal law requires divulgence, (similar to any physician, therapist or counselor):
(1) A danger to self or others
NOTE: If the Texas Health and Safety Code, Chapter 784 ever conflicts with this General Order, Chapter 784 will prevail.
B. Critical Incident Stress Management (CISM) Team

CISM is a comprehensive, systematic and multicomponent approach for the reduction and mitigation of the harmful aspects of traumatic stress in the aftermath of major incidents, disasters, or catastrophes. Due to the advent of the Incident Command System and the National Incident Management System, the Fort Worth Police Department may find it necessary to send assistance to local, regional, or national agencies who request assistance. CISM is one of the services regularly requested, therefore, standardized training is necessary and expected.

1. The Peer Support Coordinator shall obtain the necessary training from the International Critical Incident Stress Foundation (ICISF) and will ensure the Peer Support members receive basic CISM training as well.
2. The Peer Support Coordinator, or designee, will determine if CISM components should be employed following a critical or significant incident.
3. The Peer Support Coordinator shall be contacted by a Police Communications Division Supervisor when a patrol supervisor has requested the services of the Peer Support Team.

4. Notification of a Peer Support member shall be initiated by the Peer Support Coordinator directly or through the Police Communications supervisor. On-duty Peer Support members shall be given priority in selection due to the importance associated with rapid response; however, officers or employees may specifically request any peer support team member on the active list.

5. With the permission of the investigator, Peer Support members may be allowed to accompany the employee through all phases of an investigation if requested by the concerned employee. The Peer Support member status is not official and they shall take no part in the investigation. Under no circumstances shall the Peer Support member do anything that might disrupt or interfere with the investigation. The Peer Support Coordinator shall be responsible for the supervision of the Peer Support member working with the concerned employee during the initial phases of their contact.
6. Peer Support members shall not be used for regular police duties when off duty or acting in their capacity as a Peer Support member.

7. In accordance with General Order 421.02 A., a Peer Support members shall maintain confidentiality for all conversations they are a party to between sworn officers and/or employees when performing peer support and/or CISM duties. Any breach of confidentiality, outside of what is required by law, shall subject the Peer Support member to disciplinary action and expulsion from the Peer Support Team.

A. The department recognizes that each individual officer is valuable and that they are owed the appropriate care, attention, and resources that they need to overcome the challenges they are faced with in the profession of law enforcement. Encompassed within the mission of the Crisis Intervention Team (CIT) is safeguarding the welfare of our officers while maintaining their dignity, reputation, respect, and privacy. Whenever an officer or employee is experiencing a behavioral health crisis, the Crisis Intervention Team (CIT) shall respond to provide Critical Incident Stress Management Services and to support the welfare of the officer/employee and their families by referring them to available resources that will assist them in overcoming the challenges and stressors that led to the behavioral health crisis.
B. Confidentiality - All information related to services provided to officers shall be maintained as confidential pursuant to Texas Health and Safety Code Sec 784.001.
C. Definitions - Within the context of internal mental health, the following definitions apply under Texas Health and Safety Code Sec 784.001:
1. The Crisis Intervention Team is a “Crisis Response Service.”
2. Members of the Crisis Intervention Team are “Emergency Response Team Members.”
3. The actions of the Crisis Intervention Team members are “Critical Incident Stress Management Services.”
D. Officer Behavioral Health Crisis Signs:
1. Signs of an officer behavioral health concern may include: Any indicators that an officer is in need of immediate intervention to protect the safety and wellbeing of themselves and others.

a. Upon the receipt of information that an officer is experiencing a Behavioral Health Crisis, any officer or supervisor shall immediately notify the CIT Lieutenant during business hours or an on-call CIT supervisor after hours.
NOTE: Notification to CIT should be made regardless of the status of the officer’s physical health (e.g., medication, intoxication, head injury, etc.)

A. The police lead chaplain shall be appointed by the Chief of Police and is organizationally attached to the office of the Assistant Chief over the Finance and Personnel Bureau. The mission of the volunteer chaplain program is to provide non-denominational spiritual guidance, counseling and crisis intervention to the employees of the Fort Worth Police Department. Police Chaplain(s) shall demonstrate sensitivity to and respect for cultural, religion, gender, sexual orientation and physical differences when working with employees and the public.
1. The police lead chaplain shall maintain a list of representative faiths and seek to recruit clergy members from those faiths to assist in the responsibilities of the police department as needed.

2. The police lead chaplain shall be responsible for supervision, direction, and coordination with team police chaplains and, with assistance from the appropriate division(s), is responsible for background screening of team members, including but not limited to, criminal history checks, reference check, and degree and employment verification.
B. The police chaplain(s) shall be aware of the unique responsibilities of sworn and non-sworn employees.

1. The police chaplain(s) will be available to all police personnel and their family members. Because of the confidential nature of the relationship, employees are not required to notify their supervisor of the consultation; however, the officer shall call off if the consultation will cause them to miss work.

a. An employee's discussion with the chaplain concerning an addiction issue does not equate to self-referral. Refer to the City of Fort Worth Personnel Rules and Regulations, Alcohol Misuse and Drug Abuse Policy, for information related to self-referral.

2. To the extent allowed by law, any communication that a person makes to a police chaplain is on strictly confidential basis and shall not be released to any party other than the person being counseled. Records and files shall be provided the utmost security.
3. The police chaplain may be contacted either through Police Communications or directly by cell phone at any time.
C. The police chaplain(s) may not transport any person in their personal vehicle while on-duty with the police department.
D. The police chaplain(s) may ride-in with the officers to observe police operations and be on call to assist in situations where counseling or advice may be beneficial.
1. Police chaplain(s) shall not interfere with any investigation or divulge information to family members, witnesses or victims without an approval from an on-duty supervisor.
2. Police chaplain(s) shall refer all news media requests to the on-scene police supervisor or the Public Relations Office.

3. Police chaplain(s) shall complete and sign a waiver which shall be kept on file with the Patrol Bureau office. Once the waiver has been completed and filed, the member will not be required to complete the waiver or have a criminal history check for each ride-in.
E. The police chaplain shall be notified immediately by Police Communications of an employee's on-duty death or serious injury.

1. If requested by the department or the family, the lead police chaplain will assist in coordination of funeral or memorial services for in-the-line of duty deaths, and upon approval by the Assistant Chief may assist with the funeral or memorial services of any police employee.
2. If requested by the department or employee, the police chaplain(s) will be available for visitation of a hospitalized or home-bound employee.
F. Police Chaplains(s) serve at the pleasure of the Chief of Police.

1. Early Intervention (EI) is a multifaceted program designed to identify employees who may be facing professional or personal difficulties that are impacting their work performance and who may need some form of support, guidance, or assistance. The overall objective is to identify and mitigate behavior that may lead to performance issues, policy violations, and/or negatively impact employee wellness or community interactions.

2. Early Intervention is separate from the disciplinary process and shall not be used as an alternative to discipline, or to initiate any administrative investigation or discipline. An Administrative Investigation can occur concurrently with the Early Intervention process and an Early Intervention Referral does not prevent, nor take the place of anything that may result from a separate administrative investigation

a. An example could be an officer is alerted for their third instance of rudeness in the last three (3) months. The citizen involved in the most recent incident filed a formal complaint. The pattern of behavior may be sufficient, at the recommendation of the supervisor, to refer through the Early Intervention process for training, (i.e., de-escalation) or refer through the Wellness Unit for appropriate wellness resources. However, due to a formal complaint being filed, a separate, but concurrent, administrative investigation may result in a Command Level Coaching as well.

B. The Department utilizes a database (Blue Team/IAPro) that tracks potential stress-causing incidents to which officers are exposed (Accidents, Use of Force, Vehicle Pursuits, etc.). The database is designed to identify officers who may be in need of training, mentoring, coaching, counseling, or other intervention services.
C. The database provides an alert based on Department thresholds as it analyzes the previous two
(2) years, but it is up to the employee and their chain of command to make the final determination for any referral.
1. A read-only dashboard that allows for ALL POLICE employees to see specific types of incidents in the database based on rank or employee title.
a. Every employee has access to this portal, and it uses the same login information as Blue Team.
2. Uses peer analytics to compare employees within the same workgroup (i.e., West Division Patrol is only compared to other West Division officers).
3. This dashboard will need to be utilized if a threshold is surpassed and in response to an “Alert.”
4. Supervisors may view their employees’ profiles to see information about each incident.
5. Supervisors are responsible for checking the dashboard on a regular basis and at least bi-weekly.
6. If the supervisor identifies a need, the employee shall be formally referred to the Employee Assistance Program (EAP) by contacting the EAP Manager with the City.

E. It is expected that any person involved in any part of an Early Intervention review, Early Intervention or Wellness referral, or any aspect under this chapter, are to maintain standards of professional conduct as outlined in General Order 703.00, Professional Conduct, and respect the privacy of the involved employee by not sharing any information regarding these incidents except as outlined in this chapter for the purpose of reporting or as required by state and/or federal law.
A. An Early Intervention (EI) Alert will be sent out in Blue Team when the employee surpasses the established threshold for that particular incident type.

B. The threshold will be set at an identifiable limit by the Department and will be evaluated on a yearly basis. Adjustments can be made based on the current trends of the Department and only at the direction of the Chief of Police or their designee.
a. Two (2) or more pursuits with six (6) months that involve an accident that causes injuries to any person,
b. Six (6) or more use of force incidents, as defined by 306.07 (A), within six (6) months,
c. Two (2) or more chargeable accidents within six (6) months,
d. Three (3) or more citizen complaints within six (6) months, or
e. Any combination of six (6) or more of the above listed incidents within six (6) months.
C. Once the EI Alert is generated, it will be forwarded to the employee’s Deputy Chief or their designee. The Alert will indicate which specific incident(s) caused the EI Alert to be generated.

D. Upon direction from the appropriate Deputy Chief who will forward the EI Alert down the chain, the supervisor will use EIPro to thoroughly assess the identified incidents as well as any other relevant incidents in the employee’s file. The assessment shall be conducted in a manner intended to identify stress factors and gain an understanding of that employee’s performance and behavior to determine if there are any deeper concerns that need to be addressed before they impact work performance. The supervisor should also consider other factors that might be related to the alert, such as:
3. The use of both discretionary and sick time,
4. The mission and operational role of the officer’s assigned unit, and/or
5. Additional review of associated AXON footage so that the supervisor has an objective overview of the employee’s normal work behavior or performance.

E. The supervisor shall then meet with the identified employee and informally converse with the employee about the EI Alert, the review of the employee’s profile, as well as their work performance, wellness, and any other topics of discussion that may be pertinent.

1. This is a compulsory interview, but it should not appear in any manner to resemble any aspect of an Administrative Investigative interview nor imply that the potential outcome could result in disciplinary outcomes. It is imperative for the meeting to be supportive in nature and the conversation be about the potential referral options and whether either party believes a referral would be beneficial to the employee.
F. If the reviewing supervisor finds no issue or concerning behavior with the employee, the EI Alert may be closed by:
1. Documenting their finding in the “Actions Taken” field.
2. Completing and attaching the Early Intervention Supervisory Assessment form.
3. Marking the incident complete and forwarding it back through the Chain of Command up to the appropriate Deputy Chief.

G. If the reviewing supervisor feels the officer is in need of an Early Intervention Referral, they will use the “Duplicate Incident” button and duplicate the details of the EI Alert into an “EI Referral” incident type.

1. Once the Alert is duplicated, the supervisor shall close the EI Alert by indicating that the EI Referral will be generated in the “Actions Taken” section, completing and attaching the Early Intervention Supervisory Assessment form, and forwarding it through the chain to the deputy chief level.
2. If an “EI Referral” incident is created, it will document the conversation that occurred between the officer and supervisor, as well as the agreed upon referral option.

a. If the agreed upon referral is EAP, the “Action Taken” field should simply state that the officer was formally referred to EAP. The supervisor will contact the EAP Manager to ensure this process is completed correctly.
b. The Lieutenant (or two (2) levels above the involved employee) will ensure the EI Referral is reasonable and verify that it has not been attempted previously for the same issue.
H. The review, meeting, and subsequent action by the supervisor should occur within forty-five

(45) calendar days. If an extension on this timeframe is needed, the EI Alert should be forwarded to the lieutenant (or next higher rank) requesting the extension and the reason in Blue Team to document the approval or denial.

Once the supervisor believes the employee would benefit from some form of coaching, mentoring, counseling, training, or some other form of assistance, in an attempt to correct behavior that could be identified as potentially problematic, an EI Referral incident shall be generated.

A. Although the Department has a duty to assist the employee in being successful, the employee has a personal responsibility to improve and/or prevent their behavior from becoming problematic. For that reason, the employee will play an active and cooperative role in choosing their intervention option with their reviewing supervisor.
B. Intervention options fall under the following categories:

1. Coaching/Mentoring – providing personal guidance or the mentorship from a senior officer to model the desired behavior/response to a situation. This mentor could also be from a unit/rank that the officer wishes to be a member of at one point in their career so that they obtain advice on how to attain that goal.
2. Training – placing the employee in a training class that would address the issue at hand (i.e., Verbal Judo, De-escalation, etc.).

3. Temporary Reassignment – a brief “on-loan” status to allow for a temporary reprieve of their current duties in an attempt to mitigate their stress. This option would be highly dependent on staffing levels.

4. Transfer – at times, the environment might be a contributory factor, this option would allow for a temporary or permanent relocation to a different division. The relocation would initially be temporary, and the officer would have to apply for actual divisional vacancies as they open.

5. Adjust Hour Temporarily – this is similar to the Temporary Reassignment in that it would allow for a temporary hardship in order to work on creating a personal/professional life balance. This is dependent on staffing levels and should only be approximately two (2) to four (4) weeks in duration.

6. Resources for Living (formal referral) – this is commonly known as an “EAP referral.” A formal referral is not a mandated referral; the supervisor is “recommending the referral to obtain outside support.” The supervisor should seek assistance from the Wellness Unit for culturally competent counseling and other resources available through the Wellness Unit prior to exercising this option.

7. Peer Support – speak with a specially-trained coworker to seek guidance and assurance during a time of crisis who has knowledge of referral options for counseling and the ability to facilitate that referral.

8. Wellness Unit Referral – The employee will meet with a member of the Fort Worth Police Department Wellness Unit who can provide a range of wellness resources, support services, and guidance tailored to promote overall well-being and professional resilience.
C. Any further participation in an intervention option is voluntary, but highly encouraged, it will only serve to assist the employee in the future.

D. An Early Intervention Alert is not required to initiate an EI Referral. An assessment of the employee can be conducted at the discretion of the supervisor. This shall only be done objectively and fairly conducted. Any assessment would need to be discussed with the affected employee. Any referral would need to be discussed with the employee, as well, and approved by the next level up.

E. In the event that an officer is involved in a Significant Event (as detailed in General Order 421.08) and the officer appears to have difficulty coping with the incident after the fact, a supervisor is encouraged to engage the officer and can recommend the employee seek out further assistance from the Wellness Unit for culturally competent counseling and other resources that are available through the Wellness Unit. TBP 6.08

1. The employee may also directly contact the Medical Records Custodian (MRC), who should already have reported the exposure/injury, for assistance if they wish to maintain confidentiality in seeking assistance.

Significant Event reporting applies to any Department employee who during the course of their duties, is involved in a “significant” (or traumatic) event. The Department’s goal is to provide the employee with assistance from a mental health professional so the employee can learn needed coping mechanisms to process the incident effectively and to avoid delays in treatment through the Worker’s Compensation program.

A Significant Event, for the purposes of this section, is an event that exposes the employee to a physical or emotional trauma or stress that can have a negative effect on the employee’s overall well-being. TBP 6.08
Involvement in any of the following events shall require the use of Significant Event Leave:
1. Critical Police Incident – involved or directly witnessed
2. Witnessed the death of an officer or other police department employee in the line of duty
4. Any incident where the employee suffers or witnessed a fellow employee sustain a serious bodily injury likely to cause death or permanent disfigurement.
B. When an employee is exposed to such an event, Communications should be notified to contact the Wellness Unit Supervisor.
1. The Wellness Unit Supervisor will notify the on-call Wellness Unit personnel to respond to the scene to assess the affected officer or employee and provide assistance as needed.
C. A Significant Event incident will be generated in Blue Team by the involved officer’s supervisor.

1. The employee(s) who is exposed will be attached to the incident as the “involved employee.” For the purpose of the Medical Records Custodian tracking these “exposures” correctly, each employee will need to be attached to their own individual incident.
a. A brief summary providing the date, time, location and details of the event should be included in the incident. Each question that is asked on the typical “Injury IOC” should be addressed.

2. An Injury Report (DWC-1 and injury IOC), the Mandatory Referral form to Resources for Living, and the directive letter should be attached to the incident. (Documents can be found on the FWPD Portal)
3. Once the incident is complete, it should be forwarded to “EAP Coordinator” in the Blue Team system with copies sent to the Wellness Unit Supervisor and Medical Records group.

a. This action will ensure that the event is reported properly to Worker’s Comp, as well as to the EAP Coordinator, so the employee can be contacted to schedule an appointment with the appropriate professionals.
b. This action shall also initiate the Significant Event Leave/Return-to-Work process outlined below.
4. The division commander/captain/manager is responsible for ensuring this process is followed and the confidentiality of any referral.
5. The police department also encourages the family of the officer(s) to take advantage of the free (limited) counseling and support services through Resources for Living (EAP) and the Wellness Unit.

Every person has a unique response to stress and may respond differently over a period of time. Significant Event Leave is a designation of paid reprieve from regular duties for three (3) workdays after the Significant Event/Incident. It is not intended to contradict any investigative process (i.e., CPI investigation), but to facilitate prompt access to assistance while also allowing the employee time to process and cope with the Significant Event, and to assist the employee over the long term. To facilitate the use of Significant Event Leave, the following process shall be followed:

A. The Significant Event Coordinator (SEC) is the Wellness Unit Sergeant and will determine the best options and resources to utilize to address the employee’s needs. The Significant Event Coordinator and/or Liaison will be the point of contact during a Traumatic/Significant incident.
B. The leave will commence on the employee’s first regularly scheduled shift after the incident. TBP 6.08
1. Employees who, in the scope of their duties, are exposed to a Significant Event (as delineated in 421.08) are required to take Significant Event Leave. TBP 6.08

Note: Employees are required to use this time as a reprieve from the incident and duties of their job. The employee is required to not work in an off-duty capacity during this time and any loss in compensation from a regularly scheduled part-time job may be supplemented by Crime Victims Assistance. The employee should contact the Victim’s Assistance Coordinator to file the required paperwork with the State.

2. The use of Significant Event Leave will be entered by the employee’s supervisor and will not count towards “time worked” in most circumstances. Significant Event Leave will only count towards “time worked” if overtime was previously accrued within that pay week (Saturday-Friday) and the employee would otherwise lose that overtime.
a. Significant Event Leave timecode = SEL

b. If the employee has already accrued overtime within the pay week, the supervisor should notify CPPT to ensure the Significant Event Leave is coded correctly so the affected employee does not lose that overtime.

C. Significant Event Leave shall also be available to employees experiencing difficulties coping with the effects of exposure to significant events not included as those requiring the use of Significant Event Leave.
1. Employees seeking to use Significant Event Leave should inform their supervisor of the significant event(s) affecting them.
2. The supervisor will verify the employee’s exposure to the significant event and document the exposure per the significant event reporting procedure.
3. The reporting supervisor should inform the Wellness Unit Supervisor of the newly reported event.

D. During the initial three (3) days of Significant Event Leave or immediately following, if the Significant Event Coordinator determines it is in the employee’s best interest, they may order the employee to attend the Critical Incident Stress Debriefing (CISD) hosted by the Peer Support Team.
1. This will assist in “normalizing” the stresses that might be associated with the incident.
2. The Significant Event Liaison will be onsite for the CISD, but will only attend the briefing at the request of the Peer Support Coordinator and the affected officer(s).
a. The officer will code their time in attending the CISD as REG
b. The officer should inform their supervisor so that this REG time does not conflict with SEL time that is entered.

c. If the officer attends the CISD, their access to SEL will be extended to allow the them time to schedule their mental wellness check-in/crisis assessment, but not to exceed more than two (2) more working days after the CISD.

d. The maximum amount of Significant Event Leave will not exceed five (5) working days, at which point the employee will need to begin to burn their own accrued leave or obtain a modified duty status and file it with the Medical Records Custodian.

NOTE: If the EAP Manager is unable to schedule the wellness check-in/crisis assessment within the five (5) day window, the officer will return to work and be placed on Administrative Duty (desk duty) until the check-in takes place. In the exigent circumstance when multiple officers are involved in a single event that would result in a minimum staffing issue, officers from other districts, divisions, or bureaus may be utilized to ensure basic police services are not interrupted.
3. The CISD should take place only after Major Case has completed their initial interviews (if needed) so as not to taint any witness accounts of the incident.
E. Immediately following the CISD, the Liaison will meet with the affected officer and ensure the employee has contacted the EAP Manager to schedule an appointment with a licensed counselor.
1. The appointment should be scheduled on the first business day of the employee’s Significant Event Leave as stated in their directive letter.
F. The appointment with a licensed counselor is mandatory prior to returning to work.

1. This is not a Fitness for Duty evaluation. It is solely intended to ensure the officer is coping with the event in a healthy manner and to provide the officer, and possibly their family, with more coping skills to prevent the officer from developing maladaptive behavior.

2. If an employee obtains mental wellness assistance on their own outside of this process, the employee will be required to provide documentation/medical release from the provider stating the date, time, and name of the professional who was seen to the Medical Records Custodian.

G. Occupational injuries/illness is caused by exposure to factors associated with the scope of employment. Workers’ Compensation claims may be filed for physical or psychological occupational injuries.
1. Any appointments under this section that are scheduled and mandated by the Department will be at no-cost to the officer/employee.

2. Any counseling appointments made outside this mandated process or the Worker’s Compensation process will be the financial responsibility of the employee and may or may not be at a cost to the employee.
H. While on Significant Event Leave, the employee will remain available to meet with other City or Police Department officials as needed upon advice and consent of their legal counsel.

I. Once the officer has completed the wellness check-in/crisis assessment with the EAP manager and the required appointment with a licensed counselor, the Significant Event Coordinator will notify the officer’s chain of command who will then approve the officer to return to regular duty. TBP 6.08
